claims.text: Single-crystalline silicon can serve as a lattice-dominated thermal conductor.
Introducing short-range-order precipitates into single-crystalline silicon will lower its lattice thermal conductivity.
Heat transport in pure, lightly doped single-crystalline silicon is dominated by phonons and has minimal electronic contribution.
SRO precipitates can be introduced into silicon through a suitable doping or phase-separation process.
The intervention will produce dispersed SRO precipitates embedded in the crystalline silicon matrix.
SRO precipitates act as phonon-scattering centers.
Scattering by SRO precipitates reduces phonon mean free paths.
Scattering by SRO precipitates reduces phonon scattering times.
Reduced phonon mean free paths and scattering times diminish the lattice contribution to thermal conductivity.
Silicon containing SRO precipitates will have measurably lower lattice thermal conductivity than a pure control sample.
Pure, lightly doped single-crystalline silicon without SRO precipitates has relatively high lattice thermal conductivity.
The proposed effect should be most prominent when heat conduction is primarily phononic and electronic contributions are negligible.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity reduction depends on precipitate size, spacing, volume fraction, and formation method.
Ion implantation followed by annealing or controlled co-doping can be used to form the proposed precipitates in silicon.
